claims.text: The initial colloidal precursor contains Pt, Pd, Co, Cu, and Ni and is held at approximately 80 °C.
The rapid-quench batch will be cooled to below 50 °C within 1–2 minutes.
The baseline batch will be cooled gradually over one hour.
Rapid quenching at the onset of nucleation reduces atomic or precursor mobility during nanoparticle nucleation and growth.
Reduced mobility inhibits phase segregation in PtPdCoCuNi nanoparticles.
Kinetic freezing produced by rapid quenching preserves a homogeneous atomic-scale distribution of the constituent metals.
The homogeneous distribution produced by quenching is entropy-driven.
Rapid quenching promotes formation of a single-phase PtPdCoCuNi high-entropy alloy.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will contain more isolated Pt and Pd catalytic sites than gradually cooled nanoparticles.
A homogeneous single-phase structure with isolated noble-metal sites facilitates efficient charge transfer during catalysis.
A homogeneous single-phase structure with isolated noble-metal sites produces more favorable adsorption interactions during catalysis.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will exhibit better catalytic performance than gradually cooled nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles may provide higher nitrobenzene hydrogenation yields at lower reaction temperatures than the slow-cooled baseline.
Gradual cooling may provide enough atomic mobility to permit phase segregation.
Phase segregation in the gradual-cooling baseline results in less favorable catalytic-site dispersion.
The proposed quenching mechanism should apply only when quenching overlaps the critical nucleation phase.
The proposed mechanism may not apply when nucleation and relevant atomic rearrangements are substantially complete before quenching.
